original_value: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) tries to predict the polarity of a given document with respect to a given aspect entity. While neural network architectures have been successful in predicting the overall polarity of sentences, aspect-specific sentiment analysis still remains as an open problem. In this paper, we propose a novel method for integrating aspect information into the neural model. More specifically, we incorporate aspect information into the neural model by modeling word-aspect relationships. Our novel model, Aspect Fusion LSTM (AF-LSTM) learns to attend based on associative relationships between sentence words and aspect which allows our model to adaptively focus on the correct words given an aspect term. This ameliorates the flaws of other state-of-the-art models that utilize naive concatenations to model word-aspect similarity. Instead, our model adopts circular convolution and circular correlation to model the similarity between aspect and words and elegantly incorporates this within a differentiable neural attention framework. Finally, our model is end-to-end differentiable and highly related to convolution-correlation (holographic like) memories. Our proposed neural model achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets, outperforming ATAE-LSTM by 4%-5% on average across multiple datasets.

result.paraphrase: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to infer the polarity of a document with regard to a specified aspect entity. Although neural network architectures have been effective at predicting overall sentence polarity, aspect-specific sentiment analysis is still an open challenge. In this paper, we introduce a new approach for integrating aspect information into a neural model. Specifically, we embed aspect information by modeling word-aspect relationships. Our proposed Aspect Fusion LSTM (AF-LSTM) learns attention from associative links between sentence words and the aspect, enabling the model to focus adaptively on the relevant words for a given aspect term. This addresses the shortcomings of other state-of-the-art models that rely on naive concatenation to capture word-aspect similarity. Instead, our model uses circular convolution and circular correlation to represent similarity between the aspect and words, and integrates this neatly into a differentiable neural attention framework. The model is end-to-end differentiable and closely related to convolution-correlation, holographic-like memories. On benchmark datasets, our neural model achieves state-of-the-art results, beating ATAE-LSTM by an average of 4%–5% across multiple datasets.
